title: Degradation Stories & Fallback Differentiators — Messaging Drafts
content:
Purpose: Draft a compact, usable set of messaging hooks, incident narratives, and competitor counters that the GTM team can use when positioning Redwood as the safe, predictable inference partner — especially when apps need graceful degradation rather than brittle outages. This is a working doc: please add examples, customer quotes, and objections you hear in the field.

TL;DR:
- Problem customers feel: Model outages or cloud incidents translate directly to product downtime and customer trust loss; they want predictable behavior under load and clear options for degradation.
- Redwood promise: We keep apps online by automatically degrading with intent — fallback models, multi-region routing, prioritized QoS, and clear incident narratives so teams and users know what to expect.
- Differentiator: We combine deterministic runtime controls (batching, model variants, KV cache) with policy-driven routing and product-level narratives that turn incidents into controlled, transparent experiences.

Target audience:
- Engineering/ML platform leads evaluating inference vendors (primary)
- Product & biz owners at startups and mid-market companies who own uptime SLAs
- Security/compliance buyers who need auditable fallbacks and region isolation

Core messages (short form)
- Headline: "Stay online, stay useful: graceful degradation built in."
- One-liner: "When full fidelity isn’t available, Redwood keeps your features working with predictable fallbacks and observable tradeoffs so your customers get continuity instead of silence."
- Pillar messages:
  1) Predictability over magical recovery — clear SLOs for degraded modes.
  2) Control for engineering teams — choose fallback policies by route, model, or region.
  3) Observability & comms — token-level cost/latency + templated incident narratives for customers.

Example incident narratives (ready-to-adapt)
- Customer-facing (short):
  "You may notice slightly shorter or more concise responses for some features while we route traffic to alternate capacity. No action required — responses remain accurate for common queries and we’ll restore full fidelity within XX minutes. See status.redwood.com for updates."

- Enterprise incident note (for CSM/SRE to share):
  "Incident summary: regional GPU cluster experienced elevated preemption at 03:42 UTC. Redwood automatically rerouted requests to a warm secondary region and served requests using our reduced-latency variant model for low-latency features. Impact: P50/P95 latency increased by ~20% for 12 minutes; quality regression observed on <0.2% of requests that use long-form creative generation. Mitigations: automatic rollback to primary variant when capacity normalized; canary verification completed at 03:58 UTC. Action items: joint post-incident review available on request; we recommend routing your highest-value routes with 'pin model' to Dedicated for full isolation."

- Developer-facing incident blurb (Slack/email):
  "FYI: fallback engaged for route /chat/reply — serving using gen-2-small model with prefix cache enabled. We throttled low-priority background jobs. Trace links: <trace-id>. Notes: no data exfiltration; audit logs recorded per request."

Fallback taxonomy (operational language + what to communicate)
- Level 0 — Full fidelity: primary model, full context length. Communicate: normal.
- Level 1 — Fast fallback: same architecture, smaller model variant (quantized/organized for latency). Communicate: "responses may be briefer; accuracy for short answers preserved."
- Level 2 — Function-level degrade: nonessential features disabled (e.g., long creative generation, high-cost reranking). Communicate: "temporary feature reduction to ensure critical workflows stay fast."
- Level 3 — Regional failover: traffic routed to secondary region with possible higher network latency. Communicate: "you may see slightly slower responses; data residency preserved per your config."
- Level 4 — Read-only or queueing: best-effort async processing; front-end shows queued state. Communicate: "requests are queued; we will process them as capacity returns — no data loss."

Multi-region playbook (bullets for sales + CSMs)
- Default behavior: active-primary + warm-secondaries for high-tier customers.
- Fast failover: health checks at 1s, route reroute in ~5–15s for control-plane, full warmed kernels -> 60–120s for warm Node to reach steady throughput.
- Customer controls: prefer-this-region, prefer-low-latency, isolation-mode (dedicated region).
- Talking points: "Our warmed-region architecture means you get <2m recovery for most production routes, and we can guarantee isolation contracts for Dedicated customers."

Competitive signals and counters (notes from field)
- Competitor claim: "We guarantee failover because we replicate every workload everywhere."
  Our counter: replication at scale is expensive and brittle; we emphasize policy-based routing and warm pools which are much more cost-effective and produce predictable, auditable recovery characteristics.
- Competitor claim: "We never degrade — we always return full model outputs."
  Our counter: returning full model outputs under constrained capacity often manifests as long tails or timeouts. We offer explicit, tested degraded modes to keep latency bounded and user expectations managed.
- Competitor claim: "We have region redundancy" (but they provide no SLA on failover time).
  Our counter: call out our observable SLAs and warm-node median failover numbers; show customer-facing narrative templates and audit logs as tangible artifacts.

Proof points to collect (sales collateral needs)
- Benchmarks: failover time to warm region (median, 95th) across 3 recent incidents.
- Quality regressions: percentage of requests with semantic change during fallback across customer workloads.
- Cost delta: unit-cost impact of keeping warm regions vs full replication for a sample customer.
- Customer quote: ask for 1–2 customers willing to speak to how Redwood’s fallbacks prevented downtime.

Sample objection handling (reps)
- Objection: "We can build similar fallbacks ourselves."
  Response: "You could, but you'd need to build kernel selection, cache management, warm-node orchestration, policy routing, and the audit/communication pieces. Redwood delivers these with productized controls and verified runbooks so you don’t inherit the operational burden."
- Objection: "Fallbacks mean worse UX — our customers will notice."
  Response: "Fallbacks are always a tradeoff. Our playbook surfaces clear options: you can prioritize critical routes, preserve fidelity for user-facing features while throttling background work, and proactively communicate with templated language — experience shows users prefer consistent availability with slightly reduced fidelity over intermittent outages."

Customer-facing scripts (short)
- Status page tagline: "Degraded mode active — core features available, limited long-form generation."
- CSM email subject: "Update: temporary routing to alternate capacity — what this means for you"
  Body bullets: reason, impact, what we routed, expected time to normal, action for customer (none / optional pin to Dedicated).

Metric deck structure (for GTM one-pager)
1) What customers fear: downtime examples, business impacts.
2) How Redwood handles it: architecture diagram (brief), failover SLA table.
3) Numbers: P50/P95 during normal, during fallback, failover time.
4) ROI: cost avoided vs building in-house, estimated uptime delta.

Open questions / TODOs
- Collect benchmarks from infra for last 4 incidents and summarize. (Ethan)
- Draft 2–3 short customer quotes for collateral — ask CSMs for permission to publish. (Priya)
- Confirm warm-region failover median and 95th numbers and add to proof points. (Samir)
- Legal: confirm permitted incident wording for regulated customers (do we need extra approvals?). (Maya)

Notes to self / rough ideas (less formal)
- Could create a "degradation simulator" demo: let customers dial a slider from full fidelity -> minimal responses and see UX differences (good for product-led trials).
- Consider a small micro-site "How we stay online" with layered explanations for execs, engineers, and users.
- Add a short checklist for SRE teams: "When fallback engages, do these 6 things" we can ship as a PDF for customers on Dedicated.

Contact: Maya Chen (GT M) — add examples or adapt language directly in this doc.
